content: The SI system has been adopted or is in the process of being adopted worldwide. The United States remains one of the last countries to fully adopt the SI system, though its use is becoming more prevalent even there. Reproducibility of experimental results, a cornerstone of the scientific method, is facilitated by a standardized system of units. Many of these systems relied on parts of the human body or natural surroundings as measuring tools. These systems varied significantly, not only between regions but also between individuals. The original metric system, introduced in France in 1791, has since evolved into several metric systems, culminating in the current International System of Units (SI). A key feature of modern systems is standardization, with each unit having a universally recognized size. Both the Imperial and US customary units are derived from earlier English units. Some progress toward metrication has been made in the US, such as redefining basic units to align with SI units. These systems of units are based on arbitrary values formalized as standards, though some unit values occur naturally in science. Systems based on these natural values are referred to as natural units. Similarly, atomic units (au) are a convenient system used in atomic physics. Additionally, unconventional and non-standard units, such as the ton of TNT, the Hiroshima atom bomb, or the weight of an elephant, are occasionally encountered. Different systems of units are built upon distinct sets of fundamental units. The most widely used system is the International System of Units (SI), which consists of seven base units. All other SI units are derived from these base units. For most physical quantities, a unit is essential to convey their value. For instance, it is impossible to describe a specific length without referencing a unit. However, not all quantities require unique units. Using physical laws, units of certain quantities can be expressed as combinations of other units, reducing the need for a large set of base units. Derived units are created for convenience, as they can be expressed in terms of base units. The choice of base units is somewhat arbitrary, and smaller sets of base units have been defined. For example, in some systems, the electric and magnetic fields share the same unit, reflecting their interrelated nature as described by physical laws. In certain scientific fields, such systems are preferred over the SI system. The value of a physical quantity is expressed as a comparison to a unit of that quantity. For example, the value of a physical quantity ( Q ) is written as the product of a unit and a numerical factor. In formulas, the unit can be treated as a type of physical dimension, as seen in dimensional analysis. It is important to distinguish between units and standards. A unit is defined independently of physical conditions, while a standard is a physical realization of a unit that depends on specific conditions. For instance, the metre is a unit, while a metal bar representing one metre is a standard that is accurate only under certain conditions, such as a specific temperature. When performing calculations with units, they should be treated like variables. Only like terms can be added, and dividing a unit by itself results in a dimensionless value of one. Multiplying different units creates a new unit, such as metres per second (m/s) for speed. Some units have special names, but they should be treated as equivalent to their base units. For example, one newton (N) is equivalent to one kilogram metre per second squared (kg·m/s²). This equivalence allows for multiple designations of the same unit, such as surface tension being expressed as either newtons per metre (N/m) or kilograms per second squared (kg/s²). Converting a physical value from one unit to another involves comparing standard physical values. This process requires replacing the original unit with its equivalent in terms of the desired unit. For example, to convert a value from feet per second to miles per hour, one must use the relationships ( 1 , text{mile} = 5280 , text{feet} ) and ( 1 , text{hour} = 3600 , text{seconds} ). By constructing a conversion factor with a value of one, the original units can be canceled, leaving the desired units. The importance of standardized units is underscored by real-world examples. The accident claimed the lives of three crew members and five individuals on the ground, while injuring thirty-seven others.
